title: RBAC v2 design draft (working doc) — primitives, policy eval, enforcement, migration
content:
Last updated: 2025-03-07 (Kaitlyn)

This is a working draft. Expect loose ends / TODOs / conflicting notes from reviews.

Owners / review loop
- Primary: Kaitlyn Nguyen (authz implementation)
- Security owner: Marcus Lin
- Policy engine design: Jordan Lee
- Audit logging: Kevin Osei
- Control plane: Ethan Park (+ Benji Okafor)
- API gateway: Amara Diallo
- Console backend: Chloe Martin (+ Jada Williams)
- Migration/release: Connor O’Brien
- Private defaults/distribution: Hanae Suzuki (+ Fatima Noor)
- SRE workflows: Sean Gallagher (+ Rafael Mendes)

Why we’re doing this
RBAC v1 today is mostly “feature gates” + inconsistent per-service checks. Enterprise asks:
- least privilege (Billing Admin != Security Admin)
- auditability (explainable allow/deny decisions; who changed what)
- support workflows with guardrails (time-bounded, logged, approvals)
- consistent behavior across Hosted, Dedicated, Private

Scope (v2, first GA)
In-scope:
- Control plane APIs and service-to-service entry points
- Console backend endpoints + UI affordances/guardrails
- Admin/support tooling (“break-glass”, impersonation session)
- Audit log enrichment with authz decision context
- Policy bundle packaging/distribution (Hosted + Dedicated + Private)
Out-of-scope (initially):
- token-level inference authorization beyond org/project scoping (data plane)
- deep IdP refactors (SSO/SAML) except mapping groups/claims -> role assignment

Non-goals / avoid right now
- “Arbitrary ABAC” (we need a small, comprehensible model)
- Complex deny rules in customer-managed policy (see policy semantics notes)
- Big schema migrations across all services on day 1


1) Terminology + primitives (current direction)
RBAC v2 is expressed as:
- Resource: noun we protect (org, project, api_key, billing_profile, sso_config, dedicated_pool, private_cluster, audit_log_export, etc.)
- Action: verb (create/read/update/delete/rotate/revoke/assign/enable/disable/export/impersonate/etc.)
- Scope: boundary/context (org_id, project_id, deployment_id) and optionally “resource instance id”

Proposed permission naming convention
<resource>:<action> (optionally suffix for high-risk variants)
Examples:
- org:read
- org:update
- project:create
- api_key:rotate
- billing:manage
- sso:configure
- audit_log:export
- dedicated_pool:update
- support:impersonate
- support:break_glass_grant

NOTE: There is debate on where to draw resource granularity (e.g., billing_profile vs billing as one bucket). See Open Questions.

Actor types
- Human user (console/API) authenticated via Redwood identity
- Service account / API key (org-scoped, project-scoped)
- Support user (Redwood internal) + explicit support session
- Break-glass session (time-bounded elevated)


2) High-level architecture (enforcement path)
Goal: every sensitive operation has a single “truthy” enforcement point, with consistent error codes + logging.

Current direction from platform review: enforce in-service (authoritative) + optional gateway “early reject” for some routes.

Rough diagram:

   [Console UI]   [SDK/REST clients]   [Support tools]
        |                 |                 |
        v                 v                 v
   Console backend     API Gateway     Admin Gateway
        |                 |                 |
        +-------+---------+-----------------+
                |
                v
         Control plane services
         (org, projects, keys,
          billing, dedicated,
          private mgmt, etc.)
                |
                v
         Shared authz lib
        (policy fetch/cache,
         evaluation, logging)

Core design points
- Policy evaluation happens in the service that owns the action.
- Services call shared authz library with:
  - actor context (user_id, actor_type, org_id, project_id, role_ids, support_session_id)
  - resource + action + scope
  - request metadata for audit (request_id, ip, user_agent) (some of this is already in request context)
- Library returns allow/deny + reason code + policy_version used.

If we keep a “gateway check”
- Gateway may do an early reject for obviously-missing org/project membership to reduce load, but must not become the only line of defense.
- Gateway check must use the same evaluation semantics + same policy versioning, otherwise we’ll chase mismatched behavior.


3) Policy format (tracking ADR-014)
See Confluence ADR-014 (policy schema + semantics). Summary of our current draft assumptions:

- Policy bundle defines:
  - role definitions (role_id -> list of permissions)
  - optional constraints (org-scoped vs project-scoped permissions)
  - policy bundle version (semver-ish)
  - schema version

- Role assignments live in our DB (per org, per project), referencing role_ids that must exist in the bundle.

- Custom roles:
  - Phase 1: NOT customer-defined permission sets (we ship default roles; customers assign users to those)
  - Phase 2: consider custom roles as “named subsets” of existing permissions, if enterprise demands it (PM wants it, Security wants us to prove governance first)

Policy bundle object model (pseudo)
- bundle_version: "0.1.0"
- schema_version: "1"
- roles:
  - org_admin: [ ...permissions... ]
  - billing_admin: [ ... ]
  - security_admin: [ ... ]
  - developer: [ ... ]
  - read_only: [ ... ]
  - support_operator: [ ...internal-only... ]
  - support_impersonation: [ ...internal-only... ]


4) Evaluation semantics (still contentious)
We need to pick semantics that are:
- easy to explain
- hard to misconfigure
- debuggable for enterprise customers

Option A (leaning): allow-only semantics
- A request is allowed if any assigned role grants required permission for the scope.
- No explicit denies in the customer-visible policy.
Pros: simpler mental model, safer for customers.
Cons: can’t express separation-of-duty “deny” rules at policy level; must enforce with role assignment constraints (e.g., don’t allow user to have both roles) or application logic.

Option B: deny overrides
- Explicit deny rules take precedence.
Pros: more expressive.
Cons: debugging nightmare; “why denied?” becomes complicated; potential foot-guns.

Notes from architecture Slack review (paraphrased)
- Jordan: prefer allow-only for v1 of the policy language; add reason codes for missing permission.
- Marcus: allow-only is acceptable if we still have separation-of-duty constraints + strong audit evidence for role assignment changes.
- PM/Console: want UI warnings when user gets very broad roles.

Current action item
- Stick to allow-only in v0.1 policy bundle.
- Handle “can’t have both X and Y” as:
  - console UX warnings (soft)
  - optional server-side constraint list (hard?) for a short list of known conflicting roles (see Open Questions).


5) Default roles (draft)
These are placeholders; role matrix lives in Confluence page but capturing draft notes here.

Org Admin
- full management across org and all projects
- can assign roles
- can configure SSO
- can manage billing

Billing Admin
- manage payment methods, invoices, billing contacts
- view usage/cost
- cannot: manage API keys, SSO, audit log export (TBD), support sessions

Security Admin
- configure SSO/SAML, SCIM (if enabled)
- manage audit log export destinations
- view security settings + audit logs
- cannot: billing changes

Developer
- manage projects, API keys within allowed scope
- manage model rollouts within project
- cannot: org-level SSO, billing, audit export

Read-only
- view most resources + logs (but note: logs can contain sensitive config, need to classify)
- cannot mutate

Support / internal only
- support_operator: allow access to internal tooling surfaces
- support_impersonation: ability to create an impersonation session after approvals
- break_glass_grant: ability to mint a time-bounded elevated session (with additional controls)

Break-glass principle
- break-glass is a session type + separate grant process; not “just another role” assigned long-term.


6) Permission checks in services (standard)
Implementation direction (see authz check standard):
- Each sensitive endpoint must:
  1) declare required permission(s)
  2) call authz.Check(...) before performing action
  3) return standardized 403 response with reason code
  4) emit structured log fields with allow/deny + reason

Standard error response (draft)
HTTP 403
{
  "error": {
    "code": "FORBIDDEN",
    "reason": "MISSING_PERMISSION",
    "required_permission": "billing:manage",
    "scope": "org",
    "request_id": "..."
  }
}

Reason codes (draft list)
- MISSING_PERMISSION
- INVALID_SCOPE
- ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_NOT_FOUND
- POLICY_BUNDLE_NOT_AVAILABLE (should be rare; see caching)
- SUPPORT_SESSION_REQUIRED
- BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED
- EXPLICITLY_BLOCKED (reserved if we later add deny rules)

TODO: align with PR #18451 / #18541 responses so console can show “contact your admin” UX with specific permission.


7) Policy distribution + caching
Hosted/Dedicated
- Policy bundle stored in a central location (config service or blob) and loaded by services.
- Cache per org for role assignments; cache global policy bundle by version.
- Invalidation on role assignment change (org-level): publish event -> services invalidate per-org cache.

Private deployments
- Bundle shipped as a signed artifact.
- Bundle updates via installer/upgrade pipeline.
- Need version skew behavior:
  - services running bundle v0.1.0 while console backend expects v0.2.0, etc.
  - must fail safe: if permission referenced by code is missing from bundle, we should deny + emit “POLICY_PERMISSION_UNKNOWN” (or equivalent) and provide operator guidance.

Notes from Hanae/Fatima
- Air-gapped customers cannot fetch bundle from Redwood SaaS.
- We need a documented method to update bundle independent of full upgrade OR explicitly state it requires an upgrade.
- Signed bundle verification must be part of install; rotate signing keys on a schedule.

Performance constraints
- Authz check is on hot path for control plane endpoints; target p99 overhead < ~1ms per request in-service.
- Use in-memory cache + fast path: resolve role_ids -> permission bitset/hashed set.

Related PRs
- Cache + invalidation metrics: GitHub redwood/pr_18477 (WIP)


8) Audit logging: authz decision context
Audit logs should include for each sensitive action:
- actor_id, actor_type, org_id, (project_id if applicable)
- role_ids used (or role names) at evaluation time
- policy_bundle_version and schema_version
- decision: allow/deny
- decision_reason (reason code)
- required_permission
- support_session_id / break_glass_session_id (if relevant)
- request_id for correlation

Key detail: even denied requests should emit an audit event (or at minimum a structured security log). We need to decide whether this is in our main audit log stream or a separate “authz decision log” stream.

Kevin’s note
- Some customers will ingest into SIEM; we should keep fields stable + document them.
- Retention: decision logs may be noisy; propose sampling for low-risk read endpoints, but never sample “high risk” actions (billing, SSO, key rotations, break-glass).

Related PRs
- GitHub redwood/pr_18522
- GitHub audit-log-exporter/pr_88


9) Break-glass + support impersonation
Problem
- Support/SRE sometimes needs to access customer org for incident resolution.
- Enterprise wants strict controls + evidence.

Current design direction
- Impersonation is not “toggle on” for all support.
- Support user must:
  1) create a support ticket reference (Jira key) or incident id
  2) request access; approval required (who approves is still being debated)
  3) get a time-bounded session token (e.g., 60 minutes)
  4) session is scoped to a single org (and maybe a project)
  5) every action taken during session is marked with support_session_id

Break-glass is separate
- Used when normal approvals are unavailable during incident
- Must be extremely loud: paging/alerts + executive visibility

Notes from Aisha/March leadership thread (paraphrased)
- Break-glass allowed for Hosted/Dedicated; for Private deployments, allow depends on customer contract / whether customer enables “Redwood support access” at install.
- Expect alerts on every break-glass issuance.

Related PRs
- GitHub redwood/pr_18560


10) Migration plan (v1 -> v2)
We need to avoid accidental privilege loss and avoid outages. Plan is dual-eval.

Phases
1) Shadow mode (dual-eval)
- Evaluate v2 alongside v1
- Enforce v1 decision
- Emit metrics for “v2 would deny but v1 allowed” (shadow deny)
- Build dashboards by endpoint + org tier

2) Partial enforcement
- Enable enforcement by route group behind feature flag
- Start with low-risk endpoints
- Expand to sensitive endpoints after shadow-deny rate is acceptable

3) Full enforcement + remove v1 checks
- After stable period, remove v1 code paths

Notes
- Need per-tier rollout: Hosted first (internal canary orgs), then Dedicated, then Private w/ installer defaults.
- Provide escape hatch for emergencies: org-level override to revert to v1 (time-limited) ??? (Security has concerns)

Related PRs
- GitHub redwood/pr_18579 (dual evaluation)


11) Threat model notes (rough)
Threats we care about
- Privilege escalation via missing check on new endpoint
- Confused deputy: gateway authorizes based on stale role assignment; service uses different policy
- Replay/forgery of support session tokens
- Role assignment tampering (admin grants themselves broad role)
- Policy bundle downgrade/rollback in Private to re-enable permissive roles

Mitigations (draft)
- CI conformance test: new endpoints must declare permission and wire check (GitHub redwood/pr_18633)
- Cache invalidation metrics + alerts for stale role assignment
- Support/break-glass sessions signed, short TTL, bound to org_id, logged
- Audit log events for role assignment changes include before/after
- Signed policy bundles; installer refuses unsigned; record bundle version in audit events

TODO: capture full threat model in Linear ENG-5390 output.


12) Rough endpoint mapping examples (for alignment)
API key management
- api_key:create (project scope)
- api_key:rotate (project scope)
- api_key:revoke (project scope)
- api_key:list (project scope)

Billing
- billing:read
- billing:manage

SSO
- sso:read
- sso:configure

Dedicated
- dedicated_pool:read
- dedicated_pool:update
- dedicated_autoscaling:configure

Audit log export
- audit_log:read
- audit_log:export
- audit_log_export_destination:configure (maybe separate)

NOTE: We should be careful that “read” permissions don’t leak secrets (API key values, webhook secrets, SSO cert private keys). Likely need separate “read metadata” vs “read secret material” permissions.


13) Open questions / unresolved
Q1: Resource granularity for “billing” and “audit log export”
- CISO request (from Slack recap): make audit log export more restricted than general security admin? Or ensure security admin is distinct from billing admin.
- Proposal: keep audit_log:export under Security Admin only; Billing Admin only sees invoices + usage.

Q2: Should we allow a single user to have both Billing Admin and Security Admin?
- Some enterprises want separation of duties; some small orgs want simplicity.
- Proposal: allow but warn in UI; do not hard-block initially.
- Alternative: org-level setting “enforce separation of duties” (later).

Q3: “Read-only” scope — what exactly can they see?
- Console wants “read-only admin” for troubleshooting.
- Security worries about config exfiltration.
- Need sensitivity rubric from permission inventory (P0/P1/P2) to decide.

Q4: Do we need explicit “org:impersonate_member” style permissions for internal tooling?
- Might be better expressed as support session + normal permissions, rather than a bespoke action.

Q5: Multi-project orgs — role assignment precedence
- If user has org-level developer role and project-level read-only, which wins?
- With allow-only semantics, user effectively gets union. Is that acceptable? (Probably yes, but it makes “restricting” hard.)
- If we need restrict-by-project, we may need deny or a different inheritance rule.

Q6: Private deployments + support access
- Should support impersonation be disabled by default in Private?
- How do we represent “customer disallows support sessions” in policy vs config?
- Likely config flag at install time + enforced in session issuance service.

Q7: “Unknown permission” behavior
- Code requests permission that bundle doesn’t include (version skew)
- Deny + log loudly vs fail open (NO) vs service startup failure
- Proposal: deny + emit metric authz.unknown_permission and include policy_version in response logs.

Q8: Where do we store role assignments + how do we query efficiently?
- Current: role assignments in control plane DB (org_roles, project_roles)
- Services outside control plane need a read API or replicated cache.
- Proposal: central “authz assignments service” API + caching in shared lib.

Q9: How do we test end-to-end?
- Need harness that can:
  - create org + project
  - assign roles
  - call endpoints and assert allow/deny
  - assert audit log fields
- Leila to propose framework (TODO link: not yet).


14) Notes from recent reviews (raw)
2025-02-06 platform review (Ethan, Amara, Jordan)
- Keep enforcement in services; gateway optional.
- Standardize error codes; console depends on them.
- Cache: per-org assignments; add invalidation metrics to catch bugs (we already saw stale caches in staging).

2025-02-14 security review (Marcus, Kevin)
- Must log denied decisions for sensitive actions.
- Make sure role assignment changes are auditable (actor + before/after + reason).
- Break-glass needs explicit approvals + alerting.

2025-02-21 console review (Chloe, Tessa, Marissa)
- Role assignment UI needs guardrails:
  - warn when granting Org Admin
  - show “what this role can do” in plain English
  - show last modified and who modified role assignments
- When a user hits a 403, show required permission + link to docs.


15) Next steps (as of 2025-03-07)
- [Kaitlyn/Jordan] Finalize evaluation semantics text and confirm allow-only for v0.1 (align w/ ADR-014)
- [Marcus] Confirm default role matrix for SOC2 evidence needs (esp audit export)
- [Kevin] Finalize audit log schema fields + retention guidance
- [Connor] Draft rollout plan by tier + feature flags and success metrics
- [Hanae/Fatima] Private policy distribution: decide whether bundle updates can be independent of full upgrade; document version skew behavior
- [Chloe/Tessa] Console role management UX: include warnings + denied-action messaging

Appendix A: Rough “permission check” interface (pseudo)
Authz.Check(ctx, {
  actor: { type, user_id, org_id, project_id?, role_ids, support_session_id?, break_glass_session_id? },
  action: "billing:manage",
  scope: { org_id, project_id?, resource_id? },
  request: { request_id, ip, user_agent }
}) -> { allowed: bool, reason: string, policy_version: string }

Appendix B: What we need from permission inventory
Per action we need:
- service name
- endpoint / handler
- sensitivity (P0/P1/P2)
- required permission name
- scope (org/project)
- whether existing v1 check exists (missing/partial/ok)

(Inventory tracked separately; this doc is only design direction.)
